title: Understanding Trump's tariff reversals
gist: PIIE estimates that 2025-26 Trump tariff reversals forwent about $782 billion of annualized revenue (only ~$63 billion actually collected), with ~$509 billion of that being threats used as negotiating leverage, led by a $496 billion China threat, versus ~$274 billion reversed for market stability, consumer prices and company-specific Section 232 deals. Text notes the Korea threatened amount as $20.3 billion in prose but 'NA' in the table.

insights.claim: The April 2025 'Liberation Day' tariff announcement (universal 10% baseline plus country-specific reciprocal tariffs due April 9) triggered a week in which the S&P 500 fell more than 12% and 10-year Treasury yields rose about half a percentage point.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer,Katelyn Hetrick
insights.so_what: Sets the size of the market pain that forced the first reversal; a benchmark for how much equity and bond stress tariff shocks can tolerate.

insights.claim: Trump's April 9, 2025 decision to pause the reciprocal tariffs for 90 days, while keeping the 10% baseline, arrested the market rout and stock and bond markets rallied.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer,Katelyn Hetrick
insights.so_what: Market stress acted as a de facto constraint on tariff escalation, suggesting a policy 'put' tied to equity and bond selloffs.

insights.claim: Had all threatened reciprocal tariffs on 55 countries taken full effect, they would have generated about $262.7 billion of annual US tariff revenue on a static 2024-import basis; no revenue was actually collected before the pause.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer,Katelyn Hetrick
insights.so_what: Gives the scale of the revenue foregone from the market-driven reversal.

insights.claim: Most of the dollar value of tariff threats was reversed to extract foreign concessions: about $509 billion of annualized threats fell in this category, versus roughly $274 billion of threats reversed for all other reasons combined.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer,Katelyn Hetrick
insights.so_what: The authors read tariff threats primarily as bargaining chips, so headline tariff announcements should be discounted against likely deals.
insights.quote: by far the biggest effect of these tariff threats and reversals was to deliver negotiating coin for concessions by foreign partners

insights.claim: The 125% threatened tariff on Chinese imports, worth about $495.7 billion annualized, is the largest single threat and the clearest case of leverage; after Beijing retaliated, the US and China agreed on May 12, 2025 to cut to 10% (US on China side) and 30% for 90 days, leaving other US tariffs on China in place.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer,Katelyn Hetrick
insights.so_what: China de-escalation alone accounts for roughly 63% of the $782 billion total, so US-China headlines dominate tariff-revenue risk.

insights.claim: Only about $46.0 billion was actually collected on the China reciprocal tariff before reversal, against a $495.7 billion annualized threat, because the high rate was in place only April 9 to May 12, 2025.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer,Katelyn Hetrick
insights.so_what: Peak tariff rates were brief; realized revenue is far below the threatened figure, so static tariff-revenue forecasts overstate.

insights.claim: The EU Turnberry framework capped combined US tariffs on the European Union at 15%, in exchange for the EU eliminating tariffs on US industrial goods, preferential access for US seafood and agriculture, purchases of US energy, AI and semiconductor exports, and $600 billion of investment in US projects over three years.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer,Katelyn Hetrick
insights.so_what: Deal terms tie EU energy, AI and chip procurement to tariff relief, a demand channel for US exporters; EU implementation is still moving through the EU Parliament.

insights.claim: Japan's framework capped the 24% Liberation Day tariff generally at 15% (steel, aluminum and copper stay at 50%), in return for $550 billion of US investment, 100 Boeing aircraft, a 75% rise in rice imports and $8 billion of other US agricultural purchases.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer,Katelyn Hetrick
insights.so_what: Concessions are concentrated in investment pledges and big-ticket purchases, a read-through for Boeing and US agriculture.

insights.claim: South Korea's 25% threatened tariff was capped at 15% with other tariffs left in place, in exchange for $350 billion of investment in approved US projects; the article cites $20.3 billion of annualized threatened tariffs on Korean imports.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer,Katelyn Hetrick
insights.so_what: Adds to the roughly $1.5 trillion headline of foreign investment pledges (Japan, Korea, EU) whose execution is unverified.

insights.claim: The US-UK deal cut the tariff on 100,000 UK auto imports annually to 10%, removed the baseline 10% on civil aircraft and set a future MFN quota on steel and aluminum components, while the UK widened market access for US meat and ethanol.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer,Katelyn Hetrick
insights.so_what: Small in dollar terms ($1.7 billion annualized) but shows sector-specific carve-outs as the template for deals.

insights.claim: Canada remains an unresolved negotiation; annualized threatened US tariffs on Canada amount to only $1.3 billion in the authors' tally.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer,Katelyn Hetrick
insights.so_what: Canada is an open item that may produce further reversals or escalation.
insights.quote: Negotiating leverage with Canada remains a continuing saga.

insights.claim: Between April and August 2026, executive orders authorized the Commerce Secretary to negotiate company-specific Section 232 tariffs, so firms that make approved US plant-investment commitments can get reduced or eliminated tariffs on imports of pharmaceuticals, aluminum, polysilicon derivatives and drones.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer,Katelyn Hetrick
insights.so_what: Tariff exposure is becoming company-specific and negotiated; firm-level lobbying and investment pledges, not statutory rates, will drive winners and losers.

insights.claim: The terms of the company-specific Section 232 agreements have not been disclosed, even though US imports of the covered items totaled $264 billion in 2025.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer,Katelyn Hetrick
insights.so_what: Opacity makes the effective tariff burden by company unknowable; disclosure risk and favoritism are monitoring points.

insights.claim: Threatened aluminum tariffs reversed through company deals amounted to about $5.8 billion annualized, with about $1.3 billion actually collected before the reversal; aluminum was the only item in this category where tariffs were collected.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer,Katelyn Hetrick
insights.so_what: Aluminum users and producers with deals have an advantage over those without.

insights.claim: Serious research shows that tariffs are almost entirely paid by US households and business firms rather than by foreign exporters.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer,Katelyn Hetrick
insights.so_what: Tariff cost pass-through lands on domestic consumers and firms, so relief on food has an inflation and political motivation.
insights.quote: Serious research shows that tariffs are almost entirely paid by US households and business firms, not by foreign exporters.

insights.claim: After more than five years of high inflation, US households are sensitive to budget-stretching policies, which explains why food tariffs were reversed: the November 14, 2025 order exempted tropical products, beef, oranges and tomatoes from Liberation Day tariffs.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer,Katelyn Hetrick
insights.so_what: Affordability politics is a ceiling on tariffs for goods visible in grocery bills; expect further consumer-staple carve-outs.

insights.claim: The November 2025 executive order did not mention consumer prices, but the accompanying White House fact sheet did; the exemption covered $2.9 billion of annualized threatened tariffs.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer,Katelyn Hetrick
insights.so_what: Stated justification was price relief even though the order text omitted it.

insights.claim: In August 2026 Trump allowed up to 100,000 tons per month of ground beef to enter tariff-free for three months, a move aimed at relieving meat-counter prices, covering $2.1 billion of annualized threatened beef tariffs.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer,Katelyn Hetrick
insights.so_what: Short, temporary relief windows indicate beef prices as an active political pressure point.

insights.claim: Across all four categories, the authors estimate roughly $782.4 billion of annualized tariff revenue forgone through reversals, of which only about $62.9 billion was actually collected before reversal.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer,Katelyn Hetrick
insights.so_what: Realized tariff revenue from reversed measures is under 10% of the threatened amount, so the fiscal impact of the reversal cycle is small relative to headline threats.

insights.claim: The four outcomes of tariff imposition and reversal appeared in rough chronological order: financial-market stabilization, concessions from foreign governments, corporate investment pledges and lower US consumer prices on some items.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer,Katelyn Hetrick
insights.so_what: Gives a sequence for reading future tariff episodes: market stress first, then bargaining, then domestic investment and price politics.

insights.claim: The combined economic effects of the reversals are unclear; the revenue estimates are static, based on 2024 import values, and ignore changes in trade volumes, exemptions and timing of duty payments.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer,Katelyn Hetrick
insights.so_what: Treat the dollar figures as scale indicators, not forecasts of actual revenue.
insights.quote: The combined economic effects of reversals are unclear at this point
